title: Prompt library scratchpad - few-shot templates & failure cases
content:
Goal:
- Build a compact, reusable prompt library for common Redwood customer tasks (summarization, instruction-following, error-classification) with a focus on few-shot templates and documented failure modes. Quick experiments to capture high-impact low-effort wins.

Notes / context:
- These are personal scratchpad notes — not final templates. Saving iterates before adding to the shared prompt-library repo.
- Primary model targets: open models we test on Redwood hosted infra (e.g., vicuna/llama variants). Need to keep prompts model-agnostic where possible.
- Evaluation hooks: token-efficiency, exact-match for structured outputs, and manual quality checks for open-generation tasks.

Experiment 1: Instruction-normalization template (few-shot)
- Intent: normalize varying user instructions into a concise canonical action (for routing to RL/agents).
- Prompt template (few-shot):
  "You are a concise instruction normalizer. Convert the user text into a single short action phrase. Examples:
  Q: \"Please summarize the following email so I can quickly reply. The sender rambles.\"
  A: \"summarize-email\"

  Q: \"How do I reset my password — I'm locked out and need urgent access?\"
  A: \"password-reset-instructions\"

  Q: \"{{USER_INPUT}}\"
  A:"
- Shots: 2 examples (see above).
- Quick results (01-15): often works for customer support language; struggles when input contains multiple actions (e.g., "schedule meeting and write follow-up").
- Failure mode: model returns multi-sentence descriptions instead of short phrase. Workaround: add explicit instruction "Return a single hyphenated verb-noun phrase, max 3 words."

Experiment 2: Structured JSON output for entity extraction
- Intent: return a JSON with keys: entities, types, confidence. Needed for integration into downstream pipelines.
- Prompt (zero-shot + instruction):
  "Extract named entities from the text. Return a valid JSON with keys: entities (list of strings), types (list of strings same order), confidence (list of floats between 0 and 1). If no entities, return {\"entities\": [], \"types\": [], \"confidence\": []}. Do not include extraneous text."
- Observed failures: model returns trailing commentary (e.g., "I think these are..."). Also sometimes returns non-JSON (Python dict style) or uses single quotes.
- Mitigations tried: add wrapper: "Return only JSON and nothing else." Add explicit JSON schema example. Still brittle under longer context.

Few-shot example to include in library (compact):
- Example input: "Met with Dr. Allen at St. Mary Hospital on 2024-01-03. Follow-up with insurance."
- Expected output:
  {\"entities\": [\"Dr. Allen\", \"St. Mary Hospital\", \"2024-01-03\"], \"types\": [\"PERSON\", \"ORG\", \"DATE\"], \"confidence\": [0.95, 0.9, 0.88]}

Experiment 3: Summarization with length and style constraints
- Template (instruction + examples):
  "Summarize the text in one paragraph, 40-60 words, professional tone. If bullets are requested, output bullet points only.

  Example: [TEXT]
  => [SUMMARY]"
- Edge cases: When input is already short (<= 30 words), models sometimes invent extra details to fill length constraints.
- Workaround: add conditional: "If input <= 30 words, return the input unchanged but cleaned."

Failure-cases log (candidate list):
- Hallucination: invented facts/dates — often when prompt asks to "extrapolate next steps".
- Format breaks: JSON outputs contaminated with commentary.
- Instruction confusion: contradictory instructions in prompt lead to unstable outputs (e.g., "short summary" + "include 5 bullets").
- Multi-intent confusion: returns only one of multiple requested items (e.g., asked to "summarize and list action items").

Investigation notes (why these happen):
- Model attempts to be helpful: when constrained by length/style, it may synthesize plausible fill-ins.
- Few-shot examples influence output strongly; need high-quality negative examples (showing what NOT to do) for edge behaviors.

Quick experiments to run next (prio order):
1) Add 3 negative examples for JSON extraction: show model failing and then the corrected JSON. Evaluate on 100 samples.
2) Test instruction-normalizer with explicit "single hyphenated phrase" and evaluate on 200 internal support tickets. Track exact-match precision.
3) Build small automated verifier: run model output through a strict JSON parser; if parse fails, ask model to "Fix the JSON only" with the original output attached. Measure success rate after 1 fix.

Example failure case + recovery flow (rough):
- Input -> model produces non-JSON (single quotes) -> verifier: parse fails -> send follow-up prompt: "The previous output was almost valid JSON but used single quotes and trailing commas. Please convert it to valid JSON only." -> model often fixes.
- Notes: this adds latency (2 calls) but might be acceptable for batch pipelines. Evaluate p50/p95 latency impact.

Metrics to capture for each prompt/template:
- Exact-match (for structured outputs).
- BLEU or ROUGE for summarization approximations (coarse).
- Token cost per request (tokens in + tokens out).
- Failure rate by class (parse error, hallucination, format error).

To-do / next edits:
- Convert top 5 stable templates to GitHub PR format and include unit tests (examples + expected outputs).
- Share with Samira for UX review on canonical action phrases.
- Run batch test for JSON extraction on 1k synthetic samples (generate via anonymized tickets).

Random misc notes (brainstorm):
- Consider adding a micro-language for canonical actions, e.g., ACTION:add-to-calendar, ACTION:escalate-to-legal. 
- Negative example idea: show a malformed JSON and explicitly say "This is wrong because..." then show corrected version. Might train the model to self-correct.
- For models that consistently return commentary, try prefixing with a non-linguistic token boundary ("###OUTPUT###
{...}"). Some models respect a clear separator better.

Links / refs:
- Confluence: Prompt Evaluation page (linked above).
- GH: prompt-library dir - need to push templates and tests.
- Jira: JIRA-4567 for "prompt library: canonical action v1".

Logged experiments (short history):
- 2024-11-20: basic few-shot for instruction-normalizer (2 shots) — precision 0.71 on 50 tickets.
- 2024-12-05: added explicit length constraints for summarization — reduced hallucination but increased token cost.
- 2025-01-10: tried JSON-only wrapper; parse failure rate dropped from 18% to 9% but still present.

Questions / open decisions:
- How permissive should canonical action taxonomy be? (start small vs flexible strings)
- Acceptable perf tradeoff for verifier (extra call) in low-latency pipelines? Need product input.
- Should we store negative examples in the library or in a separate "failure-cases" folder to avoid contaminating positive templates?

Next checkpoints:
- Draft PR for top 3 templates by 2025-02-10.
- Share results of 1k JSON extraction run by 2025-02-24.

Notes to self:
- Save this as draft then clean up before PR. Keep examples minimal and reproducible.
- Tag tests with model/version used (we should record model id and quantization when adding to repo).
